Ensure that stop words constitute no more than 30% of the total words in your response.

message.content:
* Early empirical research (Stern, 1992; Grossman & Krueger, 1995) established the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis, suggesting an inverted-U relationship between per-capita CO2 output and national income.
  - Cross-sectional panel data spanning 22 industrialized nations confirmed pollutant concentrations peak at middle-income thresholds, declining thereafter as societies transition toward service-based economies.

* Subsequent econometric studies (Ang, 2009; Soytas et al., 2007) employed cointegration techniques to examine long-run CO2–GDP linkages across 44 heterogeneous economies.
  - Granger-causality findings revealed bidirectional feedback in wealthy nations, while unidirectional growth-to-emission causality dominated developing regions, complicating uniform policy prescriptions.

* The structural-break literature (Tang, 2015; Zhang & Zhao, 2015) challenged static EKC assumptions by incorporating regime shifts triggered by technological revolutions, trade liberalization, and energy-policy reforms.
  - Nonlinear ARDL models demonstrated that emissions thresholds shift downward when carbon-pricing mechanisms or renewable-subsidy programs operate, accelerating decoupling trajectories.

* Energy-mix decomposition studies (Ozturk & Acaravaci, 2010; Jamali et al., 2015) isolated sectoral contributions, showing fossil-fuel dependence mediates the growth–emission nexus more strongly than aggregate GDP itself.
  - Instrumental-variable estimators confirmed that electrification via coal raises CO2 intensity disproportionately, whereas wind, solar, and nuclear penetration reduce emission elasticities below unity.

* Recent machine-learning approaches (Tang, 2017; Huang et al., 2022) applied random-forest and gradient-boosting algorithms to high-dimensional macroeconomic datasets, ranking determinants of national CO2 footprints.
  - Feature-importance rankings consistently placed energy structure, industrialization level, and urbanization rate above per-capita GDP, suggesting growth quality matters more than growth magnitude for emission outcomes.

* Meta-analytical work (Mishra, 2016; Wang & Zhang, 2021) synthesized 200+ panel studies, documenting substantial heterogeneity in estimated emission elasticities of income.
  - Publication-bias corrections and methodological-quality filters narrowed confidence intervals, confirming a modest positive short-run elasticity (0.1–0.3) that turns negative beyond $25,000 per-capita income.
